problem.title: Mitigating TLS Handshake Storms on Reconnects
problem.prompt: Your Envoy ingress fleet (40 pods, 4 vCPU each) terminates 120,000 persistent mTLS/TLS 1.3 connections from 1,500 internal microservice pods. When an NLB target group or Envoy EDS/CDS reload resets connections simultaneously, all 1,500 pods immediately reconnect at ~60,000 handshakes/sec. Because TLS session tickets are disabled (`disable_stateless_session_resumption: true`) and leaf certs use RSA-2048, Envoy CPU pins at 100%, handshake latency hits 8 seconds, client timeouts trigger new reconnects, and the cluster enters a permanent handshake storm. Design a storm-proof TLS termination and reconnection architecture.

spark.summary: A simultaneous ingress/ALB rotation drops 120,000 mTLS connections; without shared TLS 1.3 session ticket keys or jittered reconnects, 60,000 full ECDHE + RSA-2048 handshakes/sec pin CPU at 100%.
spark.keyTakeaway: Enable TLS 1.3 PSK session resumption with rotated shared STEKs, switch leaf certs from RSA-2048 to ECDSA P-256, and stagger reconnects with jitter + handshake rate limits.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** An Envoy ingress fleet (**40 pods × 4 vCPU = 160 vCPU**) terminates **120,000 persistent mTLS/TLS 1.3 connections** from 1,500 pods.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts 60k/sec Asymmetric Storm vs. Shared-STEK 1-RTT PSK (1,500 Client Pods -> NLB / Reload -> Envoy (40 Pods) -> Shared STEK); Shared STEK Ring + ECDSA P-256 + Client Jitter (1,500 Pods (Jitter) -> Envoy Fleet (40x) -> SDS Secret Store -> Kernel Backlog).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Using default per-pod random STEKs (Session Ticket Encryption Keys) behind a load balancer causes 39/40 pods to reject a client's session ticket and fall back to a full handshake. Slash both per-handshake CPU cost and simultaneous reconnect rate: **Shared STEK Rotation (<= 12h)**: Distribute identical TLS 1.3 session ticket keys across all 40 Envoy pods via.

**Failure Modes & Application:** TLS handshake resilience is critical in zero-trust service meshes and edge gateways: **Envoy / Istio Service Meshes**: Protects ingress and sidecar proxies during rolling deploys or NLB target shifts.

learningJourney.title: Why TLS Handshake Storm Mitigation Matters
learningJourney.explanation: An Envoy ingress fleet (**40 pods × 4 vCPU = 160 vCPU**) terminates **120,000 persistent mTLS/TLS 1.3 connections** from 1,500 pods. When an NLB or Envoy EDS/CDS reload resets connections, all 1,500 pods reconnect at **60,000 handshakes/sec**. Without shared session tickets, full asymmetric ECDHE/RSA handshakes pin all 160 vCPUs at 100%—while security requires rotating STEKs every **<= 12 hours** and keeping mTLS active.
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Why TLS Handshake Storm Mitigation Matters works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Real-World Impact of Asymmetric Handshake Storms
learningJourney.explanation:
Full TLS handshakes are orders of magnitude more expensive than symmetric record encryption:

1. **100% CPU Saturation**: RSA-2048 signing takes ~1–2 ms CPU per handshake; 60,000/sec exceeds 160 vCPU capacity.
2. **SYN Queue Overflow**: Delayed `accept()` fills kernel `somaxconn`, dropping new connections and triggering retries.
3. **Cascading Mesh Timeout**: Healthy requests queue behind stalled TLS handshakes, tripping circuit breakers sitewide.

learningJourney.title: Naive Solution (and Why It Breaks)
learningJourney.explanation: Using default per-pod random STEKs (Session Ticket Encryption Keys) behind a load balancer causes 39/40 pods to reject a client's session ticket and fall back to a full handshake. Disabling mTLS violates zero-trust policy, and keeping RSA-2048 certs burns ~5–8x more server signing CPU than ECDSA P-256.
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Naive Solution under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise Solution: Shared Rotating STEKs, ECDSA P-256 & Jittered Reconnects
learningJourney.explanation:
Slash both per-handshake CPU cost and simultaneous reconnect rate:

- **Shared STEK Rotation (<= 12h)**: Distribute identical TLS 1.3 session ticket keys across all 40 Envoy pods via SDS/Secrets Manager (keeping current + previous key for seamless 12-hour rotation) so PSK resumption succeeds on any pod.
- **Switch RSA-2048 to ECDSA P-256**: Cuts server-side `CertificateVerify` signing CPU by ~5–8x on full handshakes.
- **Reconnect Jitter & Handshake Rate Limiting**: Configure clients with randomized connection max-age + exponential jitter so 120k sockets never drop at once, and enable Envoy `listener_filters` / admission rate limits to protect CPU.

```yaml
  max_connection_duration: 300s

overload_manager:
  refresh_interval: 0.25s
  resource_monitors:
    - name: envoy.resource_monitors.fixed_heap
      typed_config: { max_heap_size_bytes: 2147483648 }
```

```bash
openssl s_client -connect ingress-pod-a:443 -tls1_3 -sess_out /tmp/sess.pem </dev/null
openssl s_client -connect ingress-pod-b:443 -tls1_3 -sess_in /tmp/sess.pem </dev/null | grep Reused
```

learningJourney.title: Where TLS Storm Mitigation Applies in System Design
learningJourney.explanation:
TLS handshake resilience is critical in zero-trust service meshes and edge gateways:

- **Envoy / Istio Service Meshes**: Protects ingress and sidecar proxies during rolling deploys or NLB target shifts.
- **CDN & Edge PoPs**: Shared session-ticket key distribution across regional PoPs.
- **IoT & Mobile Backends**: Prevents mass-reconnect thundering herds after cell-tower or DNS failovers.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why do TLS session tickets fail to prevent a CPU storm behind a 40-pod Envoy load balancer if each pod generates its own random STEK?

options.text: Subsequent connections routed to a different Envoy pod cannot decrypt the ticket, forcing a full asymmetric handshake
options.feedback: Correct: all pods in the fleet must share the same rotating STEK (via SDS) for cross-pod PSK resumption.

options.text: TLS 1.3 prohibits session resumption when mTLS is enabled
options.feedback: TLS 1.3 supports PSK resumption with mTLS.

options.text: ECDSA P-256 certificates are incompatible with session tickets
options.feedback: ECDSA P-256 works seamlessly with TLS 1.3 session tickets.

_nextProblem.title: Multi-Leader Conflicts: Beyond Last-Write-Wins
_nextProblem.prompt: Your active-active multi-region platform runs 3 regional leaders (US-East, EU-West, AP-South) handling 15,000 writes/sec for user shopping carts, feature toggles, and inventory counters. Asynchronous cross-region replication resolves concurrent updates via Last-Write-Wins (LWW) using `System.currentTimeMillis()`. Because of a +180 ms NTP drift on an EU-West node, an EU write occurring 100 ms *after* (or *before*) a US-East write carries a higher timestamp and silently overwrites newer US-East updates—losing ~0.4% of concurrent updates (60 lost updates/sec) with zero error logs. Redesign the conflict-resolution protocol.

_problemQuestions.prompt: A user edits their bio and refreshes the page, only to see the old bio for 2 seconds because the read hit a lagging replica. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
